newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrican jail island in T-shirt trademark row.
newsitem.headline: SAfrican jail island in T-shirt trademark row.

text.p: South Africa's government was at loggerheads on Thursday with a private company which says it has trademark rights to Robben Island, where President Nelson Mandela was jailed, and is trying to sell the T-shirt.

About a dozen protesters carrying banners reading "Our heritage and dignity is not for sale" and "Don't trade on our sentiments" picketed a stall run by The Original Robben Island Trading Store in a Cape Town waterfront shopping mall on Thursday.

The stall opened on Monday and is selling T-shirts, caps, smiling toy seals in striped prison gear and "authentic hand-crafted replicas" of the key to Mandela's cell. The replica key also serves as a cork screw.
Andre Odendaal, interim administrator of the island, told Reuters the Department of Trade and Industry had ordered the trading store to cease operations.

"Robben Island is a national monument and the name is protected," Odendaal said. He said the official administration had its own plans to merchandise island souvenirs in collaboration with the private sector.
But a shareholder in the trading store, Neil du Bois, said the company had legally registered "Robben Island" as part of its trademarks.
"These were published in the government gazette as early as February," said du Bois, a retired civil servant.
"Like all South Africans, we have the right and freedom to trade and conduct our business in an open and democratic society," he said.
Products on sale carry a label reading: "A special range of products specifically designed to celebrate the new spirit of freedom and democracy which has swept South Africa."
Du Bois said his company intended to contribute a percentage of profits for the upkeep of the island, which was formally converted from a jail to a museum on January 1 this year.
About five miles into Table Bay, the island was used during the apartheid years to jail some of South Africa's most famous political activists. It has become a major tourist attraction.

Earlier this year island administrators were involved in a dispute with operators of private charter boats who tried to disembark their passengers on the island. Only state-run ferries have that right.
